node.title: Re: Order of operations
node.author: haukex
node.doctext:
The first message refers you to [doc://perlop#Terms-and-List-Operators-(Leftward)|"Terms and List Operators (Leftward)" in perlop], which says:

print ($foo & 255) + 1, "\n";

probably doesn't do what you expect at first glance. The parentheses enclose the argument list for [doc://print] which is evaluated (printing the result of $foo & 255). Then one is added to the return value of [doc://print] (usually 1). The result is something like this:

1 + 1, "\n"; # Obviously not what you meant.

To do what you meant properly, you must write:

print(($foo & 255) + 1, "\n");

See [doc://perlop#Named-Unary-Operators] for more discussion of this.

...

If any list operator (print(), etc.) or any unary operator (chdir(), etc.) is followed by a left parenthesis as the next token, the operator and arguments within parentheses are taken to be of highest precedence, just like a normal function call.

You can see how Perl is interpreting your code with [doc://B::Deparse]:

$ perl -MO=Deparse,-p -e 'print (4-1) + 2+3 * (2*2);' ((print(3) + 2) + 12);
